Note (Indicator I): The 2020 constitution's entrenched provisions concern presidential term limits — no equality clause is entrenched.

Art. 23 of the 2010 Constitution uses universal wording ('Everyone shall be equal under the Constitution and by law,' with a non-discrimination list covering ancestry, race, ethnicity, religion, etc.), satisfying the universality prong. However, no article listing permanently unamendable ('eternity clause') provisions was located in this pass — Art. 58(5) only bars suspension of certain rights during a state of emergency, which is a different (narrower, temporary) protection than entrenchment against amendment. Entrenchment status of Art. 23 is therefore unconfirmed.

Art. 26 of the 1990 Constitution (rev. 2019) guarantees equality to 'everyone' without distinction of origin, race, sex, religion, political opinion or social position — universal wording. But the entrenchment clause, Art. 156, protects only territorial integrity, the republican form of government, and secularism from revision; equality is not on that list and remains amendable via the ordinary/qualified-majority revision procedure.

Section 15 of the Constitution (1966, rev.) protects 'no person' from discrimination on grounds of race, tribe, place of origin, political opinions, colour, creed or sex — phrased universally rather than citizens-only. No provision was found that is completely unamendable; Botswana's amendment scheme distinguishes ordinary, 'entrenched,' and 'specially entrenched' sections, the latter requiring a national referendum — a demanding but existing domestic path. Whether Section 15 itself falls in the specially-entrenched tier was not confirmed.

The exact article and wording of Burkina Faso's general equality clause were not confirmed in this pass. Art. 165 bars revision only of presidential term limits, the republican form of the state, the multiparty system, and territorial integrity — not equality. Burkina Faso has also been under a military transitional charter since the 2022 coup, so the 1991 Constitution's ordinary framework is not currently the operative constitutional order.

Art. 22 of the 2018 Constitution states 'All citizens are equal before the law' — citizens-only wording, failing the universality prong regardless of entrenchment. No explicit unamendable-provisions list covering this article was found.

Arts. 1(2) and 22 of the Constitution (1980, rev. 1992) both guarantee equality specifically to 'all citizens' — citizens-only, failing the universality prong. No permanent amendment-entrenchment clause was found; Art. 108(3) only bars certain rights-related matters from popular referendum, leaving the ordinary parliamentary revision route open.

The Preamble (Principle 1) of the 1972 Constitution (rev. 2008) states 'all persons shall have equal rights and obligations' — universal wording, though it sits in the Preamble rather than a numbered rights article. Art. 64 bars amendments affecting the republican form, national unity, territorial integrity, and 'democratic principles' — not equality — so the principle remains amendable through ordinary revision.

Art. 6 of the 2016 Constitution states 'All human beings are equal before the law without distinction of race, of ethnic origin, of region, of sex, of religion, of political affiliation and of social position' — squarely universal wording. Art. 153 lists unamendable matters including (per the English rendering found) 'fundamental rights of citizens.' Flagged only tentatively: whether that entrenched phrase is a translation artifact for the broader human-rights chapter containing Art. 6, or genuinely narrower, needs resolution against the authoritative French text before any TRUE conclusion could be considered; remains UNKNOWN.

Art. 14 of the 2018 Constitution provides 'The State assures to all equality before the law without distinction of origin, of race, of sex, of religion, of political opinion or of social position' — universal wording. Art. 227 bars revision of, among other things, 'the freedoms and fundamental rights of the citizen.' As with CAR, the entrenched clause is phrased around 'the citizen' while Art. 14 itself is universal — an unresolved mismatch kept at UNKNOWN pending closer French-original review.

Art. 2 of the 2018 Constitution recognizes 'the equality of all citizens before the law' — citizens-only wording, failing the universality prong. Art. 115's entrenchment clause protects only territorial unity and internationally recognized borders, not equality.

Art. 15 of the 2015 Constitution states 'All Congolese citizens are equal before the law' — citizens-only wording, failing the universality prong. Art. 240 entrenches only the republican form and secular character of the state against revision, not equality.

Art. 11 ('All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and in rights,' UDHR-echoing, universal) sits alongside Art. 12 ('All Congolese are equal before the law,' citizens-only). Art. 220's entrenchment list protects the republican form, universal suffrage, representative government, presidential term limits, judicial independence, and pluralism, but not human rights or equality provisions; both articles remain amendable via the ordinary revision procedure.

Djibouti's 1992 Constitution (rev. 2010) has unusually strong universal wording in two places: Art. 1 and Art. 10 ('All human beings are equal before the law'). However, Art. 92's entrenchment clause protects only the existence of the state, territorial integrity, the republican form of government, and pluralist democracy — equality is not among the protected topics.

Art. 53 of the 2014 Constitution (rev. 2019) states 'Citizens are equal before the law' — citizens-only wording, which fails the universality prong regardless of entrenchment strength. Art. 226 contains an unusual one-way ratchet ('the principles of freedom and equality' may not be amended unless the amendment brings more guarantees) — one of the stronger entrenchment mechanisms found — but Egypt is disqualified by Art. 53's citizens-only phrasing.

No clear universal 'all persons equal before the law' principle was located in this pass (Art. 13(3) addresses gender equality for citizens; Art. 15(1) punishes discriminatory acts based on tribe, ethnicity, gender, religion). Art. 134 entrenches only the republican/democratic regime, national unity, and territorial integrity — not equality.

Art. 14.1 of the 1997 Constitution states 'All persons are equal under the law' — universal wording — and Art. 26.3 lists it among non-derogable rights during emergencies (a non-derogation clause, not entrenchment against amendment). Critically, the 1997 Constitution was ratified but never brought into force — Eritrea has been governed by proclamation without an operative constitution since independence — so this text is of doubtful practical relevance.

Section 20 of the 2005 Constitution states 'All persons are equal before and under the law' — universal wording with a broad protected-grounds list. Section 38 lists equality among non-derogable emergency rights (again non-derogation, not entrenchment). The full amendment chapter was not reviewed in this pass, so entrenchment status is unconfirmed; Eswatini also remains an absolute monarchy in practice, a relevant contextual caveat.

Art. 25 of the 1995 Constitution states 'All persons are equal before the law' — universal wording. The amendment procedure (Arts. 104-105) was confirmed to apply even to Chapter Three fundamental rights: it requires majority approval in all State Councils plus two-thirds in both federal Houses — a difficult, but existing, domestic path.

Art. 2 of the 1991 Constitution (rev. 2011) states the Republic 'assures equality for all citizens before the law' — citizens-only wording, failing the universality prong. Art. 117 entrenches only the republican, pluralist, and democratic character of the state, not equality.

Section 33(1) of the 1997 Constitution (rev. 2018) states 'All persons shall be equal before the law' — universal wording with a broad non-discrimination list. Section 226 is understood (per secondary sources) to entrench the Bill of Rights via supermajority-plus-referendum — a demanding but existing domestic path, disqualifying Section 33 from absolute unamendability.

Arts. 12(2) and 17(2) of the 1992 Constitution use universal wording. Art. 290 confirms Chapter 5 (Fundamental Human Rights, including these articles) is among 19 'entrenched provisions,' but entrenchment here means amendment requires a demanding referendum (≥40% turnout, ≥75% approval) — a real, if very hard, domestic path that disqualifies Ghana from TRUE.

Art. 8 of the 2010 Constitution states 'All human beings are equal before the law' — universal wording. Art. 154 entrenches the republican form, secularism, unity, separation of powers, pluralism, and presidential term limits, but not equality or the rights chapter. Guinea's 2010 Constitution has also been suspended since the September 2021 coup, under a military transitional charter.

Art. 24 of the 1984 Constitution (rev. 1996) states 'All citizens are equal before the law' — citizens-only wording, failing the universality prong. Art. 130's entrenchment list does include 'citizen rights and liberties,' the strongest rights-entrenchment language found in the survey — but since Art. 24 is citizens-only, this still fails prong (a).

Art. 4 of the 2016 Constitution states 'All Ivoirians are born and remain free and equal in rights' — nationality-based, not 'all human beings,' failing the universality prong despite UDHR-style phrasing. Art. 178 entrenches only the republican form and secularism of the state — equality is not protected in any event.

Art. 27(1) of the 2010 Constitution states 'Every person is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection and equal benefit of the law' — strongly universal wording, among the best-worded in the survey. However, Art. 255(1)(e) requires the Bill of Rights (including Art. 27) to be amended only via national referendum — a demanding but real, existing domestic procedure, which disqualifies Kenya from TRUE despite the strong wording.

Section 19 states 'Every person shall be entitled to equality before the law and to the equal protection of the law' (universal wording), reinforced by the Section 18 non-discrimination list. Lesotho distinguishes ordinary bills from 'specially entrenched' provisions (believed centered on Section 85), but the full text and whether Section 19 itself sits in an entrenched tier could not be retrieved in this pass — entrenchment status is unconfirmed.

Article 11(2)-(3) guarantees 'All persons are equal before the law' — universal wording. Amendment is governed by Article 91 (two-thirds of both houses or a 10,000-signature petition, then referendum); the one entrenched provision found, Article 93, only restricts when presidential term-limit amendments take effect and does not cover the equality clause.

Libya has no single ratified, stable permanent constitution in force: it has operated since 2011 under a repeatedly amended interim Constitutional Declaration, with a 2017 draft permanent constitution never adopted and rival authorities contesting the constitutional order. No meaningful entrenchment analysis of an equality clause is currently possible.

Article 6 provides 'All individuals are equal before the law... without discrimination founded on gender, level of instruction, wealth, origin, religious belief or opinion' — universal wording. The constitutional-revision articles were not retrievable in this pass, so whether any entrenched/eternity clause exists, and whether Article 6 falls within it, is unconfirmed.

Section 20 guarantees 'all persons... equal and effective protection against discrimination' on grounds including race, religion, and national/ethnic/social origin — universal wording. The amendment chapter (believed centered on Section 196) could not be retrieved in full, so specific entrenchment mechanics are unconfirmed.

Article 1 states 'All Malians are born and remain free and equal in rights and duties' — citizen-limited wording, not universal personhood. Amendment requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers plus a referendum (Art. 184); Article 185's eternity clause protects only the republican form, secularism, term limits, and multipartyism — not the equality clause.

Article 1 limits the equality guarantee to 'citizens.' Amendment runs through Articles 99-101; the Article 99 eternity clause protects territorial integrity, republican form, pluralist democracy, alternation of power and the presidential term limit — not the equality clause, which appears ordinarily amendable.

Section 16 protects 'no person' from discriminatory treatment — universal wording. Unusually, Section 47(2) requires a three-quarters supermajority to amend Chapter II (Fundamental Rights, containing Section 16), giving it unusually strong institutional protection — but that supermajority path still exists, so it fails the 'no path whatsoever' requirement.
Entrenched provisions concern Islam's constitutional role and the monarchy — no universal equality-by-birth clause is entrenched.

Article 35 limits the equality guarantee to 'All citizens' — citizen-limited rather than universal. The amendment framework (Art. 285/292) could not be fully verified, so whether Article 35 is entrenched is unconfirmed; the citizen-limited wording would likely disqualify it from TRUE regardless.

Art. 8 (dignity) and Art. 10(1) ("All persons shall be equal before the law") sit in Chapter 3, which Art. 131 bars from any diminishing repeal or amendment "under this Constitution" — wording unusually close to absolute, and phrased for "all persons," not citizens. The closest fit identified in this pass. Open question per §6.9.13: whether a wholly new constituent process outside "this Constitution" remains a domestic path around Art. 131 — a question comparative-law scholarship treats as genuinely unsettled for essentially every eternity clause, not one specific to Namibia. **Not asserted TRUE.** Requires a formal §6.9.8 dossier and review by qualified Namibian counsel.

Article 8 assures 'all equality before the law without distinction of sex, or of social, racial, ethnic or religious origin' — universal wording. Amendment requires supermajorities under Articles 173-174; Article 175's eternity clause protects the republican form, multiparty system, and separation of state and religion — the general equality clause is not among the protected items.

Section 42 limits the equality/non-discrimination guarantee to 'a citizen of Nigeria' — citizen-limited, not universal. Chapter IV (including Section 42) requires four-fifths of each National Assembly house plus two-thirds of State Houses of Assembly to amend — a strong but still-existing domestic amendment path.

Article 15 states 'All persons are equal before the law,' and Article 16 adds an unusually comprehensive non-discrimination list explicitly including 'ancestry' — among the most textually favorable clauses found. However, the amendment/entrenchment provisions could not be reliably retrieved or confirmed in this pass, so entrenchment status remains genuinely unconfirmed.

Article 15 limits the equality clause to 'All citizens' — citizen-limited, not universal personhood. Article 154 lists nine unrevisable matters including 'citizens' rights and freedoms,' which could arguably extend to Article 15, though the clause itself remains citizen-limited wording.

Article 1 limits equality to 'all the citizens,' but Article 7 separately states 'All human beings are equal before the law' — genuinely universal wording, one of the stronger cases found. However, Article 103's eternity clause protects only the republican form, mode of presidential election, and term limits/duration — Article 7 is not on that list and is amendable via the ordinary procedure.

Article 27 provides 'Every person has a right to equal protection of the law... without discrimination on any ground' — universal, open-ended wording. The amendment procedure (believed centered on Article 91) could not be retrieved in this pass, so entrenchment status is unconfirmed.

Section 27 protects 'no person' from discriminatory treatment (universal), while Section 8(2)(a) separately frames it as 'every citizen shall have equality of rights' (citizen-limited) — mixed signals on scope. The amendment chapter was not retrievable in this pass, so the entrenchment procedure and whether either provision is protected remain unconfirmed.

Article 11's primary clause is citizen-limited ('All citizens... shall have equal rights'), though it separately requires government non-discrimination on a broad list including ethnicity, tribe, religion and birth. Specific amendment-majority requirements and any entrenched provisions could not be confirmed; Somalia's constitution also remains formally provisional/under ongoing review.

s.9 ("everyone is equal before the law") and s.10 ("everyone has inherent dignity") use fully universal wording, among the strongest found anywhere — but amendment requires only a 75% National Assembly + 6-province vote (s.74), an extraordinarily high but real domestic path, not an absolute bar. Fails §6.9.2(b)'s "cannot be touched by any procedure" test.

Article 48 of the 2011 Transitional Constitution states 'People are equal before the law... without discrimination... on the basis of ethnicity, colour, gender, language, religious faith, political opinion, racial or ethnic origin' — universal, comprehensive wording. Amendment under Article 67 requires only a two-thirds legislative majority with no referendum or entrenchment requirement found — more easily amendable than most peer constitutions. South Sudan's promised permanent constitution remains unfinished as of 2026.

The 2019 transitional charter contains a similarly worded Article 48, amendable via two-thirds of the Transitional Legislative Council with no eternity clause identified. More fundamentally, Sudan's constitutional order has been disrupted by the October 2021 military takeover and the civil war ongoing since April 2023, so there is currently no stable, functioning constitutional document to assess.

Article 13(1) states 'All persons are equal before the law' — universal wording, confirmed from the official text. Amendment is governed by Article 98 and the Second Schedule (two-thirds thresholds); Article 13 was not identified as falling within either entrenched list, so it appears amendable through the ordinary procedure.

Article 2 assures 'the equality before the law of all citizens' — citizen-limited, not universal personhood. Amendment (Art. 144) requires a four-fifths majority or two-thirds plus referendum; the eternity clause protects only the republican form and secular character of the state — not equality.

Articles 19 and 23 frame equality in terms of 'citizens' — citizen-limited. Amendment (Arts. 136-137) requires a two-thirds vote across two readings or referendum; Article 136's eternity clause protects only the republican system and term limits. Article 55 offers some broader protection against 'prejudicing the gains and freedoms of human rights,' but this is not an absolute eternity clause for the equality article specifically.

Article 21 states 'All persons are equal before and under the law' — universal wording. Uganda's amendment scheme has an ordinary tier, a two-thirds tier (Art. 259), and a 'particularly entrenched' tier requiring both two-thirds and a national referendum (Art. 260); whether Article 21 falls in the referendum-entrenched tier could not be confirmed with a specific citation, a genuine research gap.

Article 23 protects 'no person' from discriminatory treatment — universal wording, phrased as non-discrimination. Amendments to Part III (Bill of Rights, containing Article 23) require a national referendum with at least 50% of registered voters' support — strong entrenchment, but still an existing domestic path.

Section 56 states 'All persons are equal before the law' — universal wording with an extensive protected-grounds list. The amendment procedure for the Declaration of Rights chapter (believed to require a two-thirds vote plus national referendum) could not be retrieved in full, so specific entrenchment mechanics for Section 56 are unconfirmed rather than assumed.

The 2004 constitution (whose current force is itself unsettled given events since 2021, which are outside the scope of this table) entrenched only Islam's constitutional role and republican form; its equality clause (Art. 22) was explicitly citizens-only ("citizens of Afghanistan, man and woman, have equal rights") and was not entrenched in any event.

Article 28 grants equality before the law to 'everyone,' and Article 29 bars discrimination on grounds including ethnic/social origin, national-minority status, birth, and religion. Article 80 states the 'essence' of Chapter 2's fundamental-rights provisions (including Arts. 28-29) 'shall be inviolable' — an unusual eternity-style clause — but Chapter 2 can still be amended via constitutional referendum, and nothing bars a referendum from first narrowing Article 80 itself, so a domestic path remains open.

Article 25 grants equality before the law to 'everyone,' with a broad grounds list. Article 71(5) states no constitutional provision 'may be used to abolish human rights and civil liberties,' but this reads as an interpretive/anti-abuse rule rather than a formal bar on amendment, and the constitution is amendable by referendum under Article 3.

Article 18 says 'people are equal in human dignity,' but the operative before-the-law equality guarantee is limited to 'citizens.' Article 120(3)-(4) entrenches the monarchy, succession, and 'the principles of freedom and equality,' but since the underlying clause is citizens-only, this entrenchment doesn't satisfy the test.

Article 27 limits equality before the law to 'citizens,' and Article 28 lists only religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth as prohibited grounds. Article 7B is one of the strongest entrenchment clauses anywhere, barring amendment of Parts I-III (including Arts. 27-28) — but because the protected clause is citizens-only, this near-total entrenchment does not satisfy the universal-wording prong.

Article 7 states 'All persons are equal before the law' — reasonably universal wording. No eternity clause protects this article; amendment uses the ordinary two-thirds joint-sitting procedure, with only monarchy-status matters requiring a referendum.

The 1959 Constitution (as amended) contains no general equality-before-the-law clause at all. Article 85(1) additionally lets the Sultan amend 'any of the provisions of this Constitution including this Article' by proclamation, so nothing — including the amendment power itself — is entrenched. Fails both prongs clearly.

Article 31 limits equality before the law to 'Khmer citizens' — failing the 'all persons' requirement. Articles 17 and 153 entrench the constitutional-monarchy system and multiparty democracy against amendment, but not the (citizens-only) equality clause.

Article 33 limits equality before the law to 'citizens'; Article 4 separately guarantees equality 'of all nationalities' as groups, not universal personhood. No eternity clause exists — amendments require only a two-thirds NPC majority, and the constitution has been amended repeatedly.

Article 28(1)-(2) is unusually strong: 'All persons are equal before the law, the administration and justice' with a broad grounds list including birth — squarely universal wording. Cyprus also has one of the strongest formal entrenchment mechanisms found: Article 182 declares 48 'basic articles' (Annex III) outside the amendment power altogether. Whether Article 28 itself is among those 48 protected basic articles could not be confirmed in this pass — flagged as the strongest structural candidate found, but UNKNOWN pending that confirmation.

Article 11(1) grants equality before the law to 'all persons' (not citizens-only) with a broad grounds list — strong universal wording. No eternity clause or entrenched-provisions chapter was found; amendments, including to the human-rights chapter, require only a two-thirds parliamentary majority, leaving an ordinary domestic amendment path open.

Art. 14 ("the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law") is universal wording, but its practical unamendability rests entirely on the judicially-created "basic structure doctrine" (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), not a textual entrenchment clause — Art. 368 (the amendment power) itself contains no textual entrenchment list. Fails §6.9.2/§6.9.3's textual/domestic-procedure framing as currently understood.

Article 27(1) limits equality before the law/government to 'citizens,' while Articles 28D(1) and 28I(2) extend broader protection to 'every person' against discrimination 'on any grounds whatsoever' — a split framing that doesn't cleanly satisfy the universal wording requirement. Article 37(5) entrenches only the unitary form of the state, not the equality provisions.

Article 19 addresses 'all people of Iran, whatever the ethnic group or tribe,' while Article 20's fuller equal-protection guarantee is limited to 'citizens' and conditioned on conformity 'with Islamic criteria.' Article 12 entrenches Twelver Shi'a Islam as 'eternally immutable,' but no equivalent entrenchment protects the equality clauses themselves.

Article 14 provides equality for 'Iraqis' — broad grounds but limited to Iraqis, not all persons. Article 126 gives Article 14 heightened protection (two electoral terms, two-thirds vote, referendum, presidential ratification to amend) — a very demanding procedure, but not an absolute bar.

Israel has no single codified constitution; it relies on Basic Laws. No Basic Law or statute currently contains a general 'all persons equal before the law' guarantee — courts have inferred elements of equality from the Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty's dignity clause, but a standalone universal equality provision does not exist in enacted law. Since no such clause exists, there is nothing to be entrenched.

Article 14 provides 'All of the people are equal under the law' — satisfies universal wording, though ethnicity/ancestry are covered only loosely via 'family origin.' Article 96 subjects the entire constitution to amendment via a two-thirds Diet vote plus referendum; no provision, including Article 14, is designated unamendable.
Article 6(1) provides equality for 'Jordanians' — limited to citizens, with a narrower grounds list (race, language, religion only). No entrenched-provisions clause covering Article 6 was found.

Article 14 provides 'Everyone shall be equal before the law and court' — strongly universal wording with broad grounds. The entrenchment clause, Article 91(2), protects only state independence, unitary status, territorial integrity, the form of government, and the First President's status — not Article 14, which remains ordinarily amendable.

Article 29 provides 'People are equal in human dignity, and equal before the law in public rights and duties' — phrased around 'people,' reasonably universal. Article 175 bars any proposed revision to provisions on the Amiri system and 'the principles of liberty and equality' except to raise the level of guarantees — a strong one-directional entrenchment. It is unconfirmed whether Article 175 protects itself from prior repeal (which could allow a two-step circumvention), so an absolute bar cannot be confirmed — flagged as one of the strongest mechanisms found, but UNKNOWN.

Article 24 provides 'everyone' is 'equal before the law and the courts' — broad, universal wording. No eternity clause was found; Article 56(2)'s bar on laws that 'abolish or diminish human rights' constrains ordinary legislation, not constitutional amendment, and no provisions are listed as unamendable.

Article 35 limits equality before the law to 'Lao citizens' — citizens-only wording. No unamendable provisions were identified; the National Assembly has unrestricted amendment power by a two-thirds vote.

Article 7 provides equality for 'All Lebanese' — limited to nationals, without an enumerated grounds list. No formal entrenchment protects Article 7; ordinary amendment procedures apply without carve-outs.

Article 8(1) provides 'All persons are equal before the law' — genuinely universal wording with a solid grounds list. However, Article 159(5) entrenches only Article 1, Article 153 (special position of Malays/Bumiputera) and Article 181 (Rulers' sovereignty) — Article 8 is not on that protected list and has in fact been amended before.

Article 20 ('every individual is equal before and under the law') and Article 17(1) use universal, non-citizen-limited wording. But the only clearly entrenched feature is Article 10 (Islam as state religion), not the equality clause, and the People's Majlis can amend the constitution by ordinary procedure under Article 70(2)(a) with no unamendable-provision list found.

Article 14 ('All persons lawfully residing within Mongolia shall be equal before the law and the courts') is universal wording. However, the constitution has no eternity clause, and Articles 68-69 give a clear domestic amendment path (3/4 State Great Hural vote, with a referendum option).

Article 21(a) limits equality to citizens, failing the universal-wording prong outright. Article 6(f) irrevocably bars secession but says nothing about equality. Since the 2021 coup the charter's normal operation is effectively suspended in practice under military SAC rule.

Article 18's first sentence is citizens-only, with only a second, ambiguous 'person' sentence on equal protection. Article 274(1) entrenches only sovereignty, territorial integrity, independence, and popular sovereignty — the equality article is not on that list, and ordinary amendment needs just 2/3 of both federal houses.

Article 65 ('Citizens enjoy equal rights in all spheres') is citizens-only, failing prong (a) regardless of amendability. Article 97 allows amendment by a 2/3 Supreme People's Assembly vote, and no provision is declared formally unamendable.

Article 17 of the Basic Statute ('All Citizens are equal before the Law...') is citizens-only. Article 81 requires amendment 'in the manner in which it was promulgated,' i.e. by a new Royal Decree — an ever-present domestic (executive) amendment path.

Article 25(1) ('All citizens are equal before law') is citizens-only. The Objectives Resolution and Islamic provisions have elevated status, but none formally entrenches Article 25, which is amendable via a 2/3 vote of Majlis-e-Shoora; Pakistan's 'basic structure doctrine' remains judicially contested, not settled law.

Article III, Section 1 equal protection covers 'all persons' — universal wording. But Article XVII offers three live amendment routes, each requiring only referendum ratification, and no provision — including equal protection — is declared unamendable; Philippine jurisprudence has not adopted an Indian-style unamendable 'basic structure' bar.

Article 35 ('People are equal before the law...') is genuinely universal wording. Article 146 provides that rights/freedoms provisions (including Art. 35) 'may not be amended except to grant the citizens more rights and freedoms' — a one-way ratchet against narrowing. The strongest case surfaced in this survey, but it still permits expansion-direction amendment and its enforcement is unverified, so it stays UNKNOWN.

Saudi Arabia has no rigid written constitution; the Basic Law of Governance (1992) is a Royal Decree. Article 8 references 'equality' only as a governance premise 'in accordance with the Islamic Shari'ah.' Article 83 lets the Law be amended by another Royal Decree, a permanent, unrestricted domestic amendment path.

Article 12(1) is universal ('All persons are equal before the law'). There is no eternity/entrenchment clause of the relevant kind; Article 12 can be amended, like most provisions, by an ordinary 2/3 parliamentary majority.

Article 11 ('All citizens are equal before the law...') is citizens-only, failing prong (a). The constitution's one entrenched feature (Art. 128(2)) only blocks a sitting president from extending their own term, unrelated to equality.

Article 12(1) is phrased universally ('All persons are equal before the law'). Article 83 entrenches only Articles 1-3, 6-11, and 83 itself — Article 12 is not on that list, so it is amendable by an ordinary 2/3 parliamentary vote alone.

The 2012 Ba'athist constitution has been superseded by a March 2025 interim Constitutional Declaration governing a transition; secondary sources report it guarantees legal equality for citizens (citizens-framed, not universal). Given the transitional, contested constitutional order, this defaults to UNKNOWN.

Article 17 is universal wording ('All are equal before the law and court... regardless of... nationality, race, gender, language, religious beliefs'). Article 100 entrenches only the republican form, territorial integrity, and the state's democratic/secular/social character — equality is not on that list.

Section 27 is universal ('All persons are equal before the law'). Section 255 bars only amendments changing the democratic regime with the King as Head of State or the unitary form of the state; equality is not part of that entrenched core.

Art. 16 reads "all citizens are equal before the law," then separately "no one may be discriminated against..." — a citizens-first/universal-second structure. Whether either clause, or the universal human-dignity language in Art. 1/preamble, is covered by the constitution's limits-of-revision article was not confirmed in this pass.
Art. 4 entrenches Arts. 1–3 (republican form, state characteristics, territorial/language/flag/capital integrity) — no equality clause is entrenched at all. Art. 10 (equality) is not protected.
Article 28 protects 'a person and a citizen' with broad, largely universal wording. Article 141 entrenches only the presidential-republic form of government — equality is not on that list.

Article 25 states 'All persons are equal in law,' though the same article narrows its anti-discrimination clause to 'no distinction among the citizens of the UAE,' creating ambiguity. No provision anywhere is declared unamendable, and an ordinary amendment route exists.

Article 19 of the 2023 Constitution is citizens-only, failing prong (a). Article 16 gives heightened interpretive protection to the Fundamental Principles chapter, but this is not a formal unamendability clause.
Article 16 of the 2013 Constitution is citizens-only, failing prong (a). No article is declared unamendable; Article 120 sets a 2/3 National Assembly supermajority as the amendment procedure.

Article 41 of the 1991 Constitution is citizens-only, failing prong (a). Article 158 entrenches a long list of other articles requiring 3/4 House approval plus referendum, but Article 41 is not among them; Yemen's ongoing civil war further makes the document's operative status contested.

Article 18 states 'All are equal before the law' and bars unjust discrimination on grounds including sex, race, religion, ethnicity, and other status — universal wording, not citizens-only. Amendment (Articles 177-178) is by 2/3 Assembly vote, with certain provisions additionally subject to referendum if requested by 1/5 of MPs or 50,000 voters — but no provision, including Article 18, is placed beyond any domestic amendment path.

Article 6 provides universal equality ('All persons are equal before the law... on grounds of birth, race, sex, origin, religion, opinions or any other personal or social condition'), satisfying the universal-wording prong. Articles 105-107 set out an ordinary (if demanding) amendment procedure with no eternity clause identified anywhere in the text, so Article 6 remains fully amendable.

Article 7(1) of the Federal Constitutional Law reads 'All nationals are equal before the law,' citizens-only wording, already failing prong (a). Article 44 sets an amendment procedure with no explicit eternity clause, so even a broader equality clause would remain amendable.

Article 22 states 'All shall be equal before the law' in universal terms. Article 140 places Sections I, II (containing Art. 22), IV, and VIII into a category amendable only by national referendum — a real, distinctive entrenchment — but a referendum is still a domestic amendment procedure (and one Belarus has in fact used), so this fails prong (b).

Article 10 ('Belgians are equal before the law') is citizens-only; the broader Article 11 non-discrimination guarantee is phrased around Belgians' rights rather than a freestanding universal clause. Article 195's amendment procedure has no identified eternity clause — all articles are formally revisable.

Art. II(4) guarantees non-discrimination, naming "birth" explicitly, to "all persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Art. X(2) bars any amendment that eliminates or diminishes Art. II rights and separately bars amending that entrenchment clause itself — closing the obvious loophole. The second-closest fit identified in this pass. The constitution is Annex 4 to an international peace agreement, adding a further layer of rigidity, but this also raises open questions about how it interacts with the international instrument it is annexed to. **Not asserted TRUE.** Requires a formal §6.9.8 dossier and review by qualified Bosnian counsel.

Core provisions require a specially-elected Grand National Assembly rather than the ordinary parliament — an extraordinarily demanding procedure, but a real, existing domestic path, not an absolute bar.

Article 26 provides that 'All citizens... and aliens shall be equal before the courts, government bodies...' — broader than citizens-only since aliens are expressly included, though phrased institutionally. Amendment is by 2/3 Parliament vote with no eternity clause.

Constitution Art. 9(2) bars changing "essential attributes of the democratic, law-observing state" — a broad principle, not a textual equality clause. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (part of the constitutional order) opens with "All people are free and equal in their dignity and rights" — universal wording — but its protection under Art. 9(2)'s "material core" rests on Constitutional Court doctrine (Melčák, 2009), not an explicit textual designation, structurally closer to India's judicial basic-structure doctrine than to a clean textual eternity clause.

Denmark's Grundlov notably lacks a general equality-before-the-law clause at all — the closest provision, Section 70, only bars deprivation of civil/political rights 'on account of creed or descent,' a narrow guarantee. Amendment (Section 88) requires passage, an intervening election, repassage, and a referendum; no eternity clause exists.

Article 12 states 'Everyone is equal before the law,' with Article 9 confirming rights apply equally to citizens, foreign citizens, and stateless persons — universal wording. Article 162 protects Chapters I and XV by referendum-only amendment, but Article 12 sits in Chapter II, outside that specially-protected set, and is amendable through ordinary Riigikogu procedures.

Section 6 states 'Everyone is equal before the law' and bars discrimination on grounds including origin, language, religion, and conviction — universal wording. Amendment (Section 73) requires a demanding but entirely ordinary procedure; no eternity clause exists.
Art. 89 entrenches only the republican form of government — no rights content of any kind is entrenched.

Art. 79(3) GG entrenches Art. 1 (human dignity, universal wording) and Art. 20 — but not Art. 3, the general equality clause, which is not on the entrenched list. Fails §6.9.2(a)/(b) on the current text: dignity is entrenched, equality as such is not. Separately, Art. 146 GG contemplates a new constitution "freely adopted by the German people," which scholars debate as a possible domestic path around Art. 79(3) for a wholesale replacement.

Art. 110 entrenches, among other things, Art. 4(1): "All Greeks are equal before the law" — explicitly citizens-only. Art. 5(2)'s broader "all persons... irrespective of nationality" clause is a liberty/security guarantee, not an equality clause, and is only partially on the Art. 110 list. Fails §6.9.2(b)'s "all human beings" requirement on its entrenched text.

Article XV(1) states 'Everyone shall be equal before the law. Every human being shall have legal capacity' — strongly universal wording. Amendment (Article S) requires only a 2/3 National Assembly vote; no article is formally placed outside that ordinary amendment power, and Article XV(1) has in fact been amended before.

Article 65 provides 'Everyone shall be equal before the law and enjoy human rights irrespective of sex, religion, opinion, national origin, race, colour, property, birth or status in general' — strongly universal. Amendment (Article 79) requires passage, dissolution, election, and repassage — no eternity clause exists, so Article 65 remains fully amendable.

Article 40.1 states 'All citizens shall, as human persons, be held equal before the law' — textually citizens-only, a likely fail on the universal-wording prong. Ireland has no unamendable constitutional core: every provision is amendable by ordinary bill plus simple-majority referendum under Article 46, used over 30 times.
Art. 139 entrenches only the republican form of government — no rights content of any kind is entrenched.

Article 91 of the Satversme states 'All human beings in Latvia shall be equal before the law and the courts' — strongly universal wording. Article 77's partial entrenchment (referendum for Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, or 6) does not include Article 91, so it is amendable by the ordinary 2/3 Saeima procedure without any referendum requirement.

Article 31 is phrased as 'All Liechtenstein citizens are equal before the law' — citizens-only, failing prong (a). Amendment can occur via the Landtag or via popular initiative/referendum, with the reigning Prince holding an absolute sanction/veto — a political check, not a legal entrenchment exempting any clause from the domestic amendment process.

Article 29 states 'All persons shall be equal before the law' and bars privileges/discrimination on broad grounds — clearly universal wording. Article 148's eternity clause protects Chapters I and XIV, but Article 29 sits in Chapter II, outside that specially-protected set, and is amendable by the ordinary Article 147 procedure.

Luxembourg's constitution (replaced 1 July 2023) is understood to carry forward a citizens-limited equal-treatment guarantee from the prior 1868 text's Article 11(2) ('Luxembourgers are equal before the law'). Revision has always proceeded under an ordinary (if deliberately slow) mechanism, and no eternity clause or unamendable core exists in Luxembourg constitutional law; confidence on the new constitution's exact article numbering is lower than for other countries in this batch.

Art. 32 protects fundamental rights of 'every person in Malta' (universal wording), reinforced by the Art. 45 non-discrimination clause. Art. 66 makes these provisions amendable by a two-thirds majority of the House of Representatives — no referendum or constituent assembly needed — a live domestic amendment path.

Art. 16 equality clause covers 'all citizens of the Republic of Moldova' — citizens only, failing universality alone. Art. 142 entrenches only sovereignty, independence, unity and permanent neutrality; Art. 16 is not on that entrenched list and remains changeable via the ordinary Art. 143 procedure.

Art. 17 states 'All Monegasques are equal before the law' — limited to nationals, failing the universality prong outright. Amendment requires joint agreement of the Prince and a two-thirds National Council vote; no provision is declared unamendable.

Art. 17 provides universal wording ('All shall be deemed equal before the law, regardless of any particularity or personal feature'), but is not among the specially entrenched articles (Art. 157: Arts. 1-4, 12, 13, 15, 157). Montenegro has no true eternity clause — even entrenched articles can be changed via a three-fifths-of-voters referendum.

Art. 1 provides 'All persons in the Netherlands shall be treated equally in equal circumstances,' broadly universal, but the Constitution contains no eternity clause whatsoever — any provision can be amended through the ordinary (if rigorous) Chapter 8 procedure.

Art. 9 limits equality to 'Citizens of the Republic of Macedonia' — failing the universal-persons prong. Amendment XVIII specially entrenches Art. 9 via a double/Badinter majority, but this is still a live domestic amendment mechanism, not an absolute bar.

Norwegian constitutional theory has long debated an unwritten, non-enumerated eternity principle protecting the Constitution's "spirit," but it is contested, undefined in scope, and not judicially enforced in practice — and does not map onto a specific, identified universal equality-by-birth clause.

Art. 32(1)-(2) uses universal language ('All persons shall be equal before the law... No one shall be discriminated against for any reason whatsoever'). Poland has no eternity clause: Art. 235 allows amendment of any chapter via a two-thirds Sejm / absolute-majority Senate vote, with only an optional confirmatory referendum for certain chapters.

Art. 288's limits-of-revision clause is consistently described in secondary sources as protecting "the rights, freedoms and guarantees of citizens" — citizens-only phrasing, though ordinary constitutional law (Art. 15) extends most individual rights to foreign/stateless residents by a separate, non-entrenched mechanism.
Art. 152 entrenches "citizens' fundamental rights and freedoms" — explicitly citizens-only, not universal.

Article 19 guarantees equality of rights and freedoms of man and citizen regardless of sex, race, nationality, language, origin, property/official status, place of residence, religion, convictions, or other circumstances — universal 'human and citizen' wording. Article 135 places Chapters 1, 2 (containing Art. 19), and 9 beyond the ordinary Federal Assembly amendment power, but Article 135 itself provides a domestic path: with 3/5 support in both chambers, a Constitutional Assembly is convened, which may draft a new constitution adopted by the Assembly itself or by national referendum. This constituent-assembly route is a real, existing (if rarely used) domestic mechanism, structurally analogous to Bulgaria's Grand National Assembly path, so Russia fails prong (b) despite satisfying prong (a).

Art. 4 of the 1974 Declaration states 'All shall be equal before the law, without any distinction based on sex or personal, economic, social, political and religious status' — broadly universal, though it does not explicitly enumerate ethnicity/ancestry. No eternity clause exists; Art. 17 allows revision by a two-thirds Great and General Council vote or by absolute majority plus referendum.

Art. 21 uses universal wording ('All are equal before the Constitution and law'). Art. 203 gives Part Two (including Art. 21) heightened protection requiring a two-thirds vote and generally a confirming referendum — but that referendum route is itself a domestic amendment procedure, so no absolute bar exists.

Art. 12 extends basic rights to 'everyone... regardless of sex, race, colour of skin, language, faith and religion' — clearly universal wording. Slovakia's Constitution contains no eternity clause at all; any provision can be amended via an ordinary three-fifths parliamentary supermajority.

Art. 14 guarantees equal human rights 'irrespective of national origin, race, sex, language, religion... All are equal before the law' — strongly universal wording. No eternity clause exists anywhere; Arts. 168-171 permit amendment of any provision via an ordinary two-thirds National Assembly vote.

Art. 14 states 'Spaniards are equal before the law' — limited to Spanish nationals, disqualifying it from the universal-wording prong regardless of the rigid Art. 168 'total revision' procedure (which is demanding but still an existing domestic procedure with no absolute bar).

Sweden's equality language is split: a non-justiciable objective (Ch. 1, Art. 2) versus a narrower, legislatively-framed anti-discrimination rule (Ch. 2, Art. 12) rather than a general 'equal before the law for all persons' clause. No eternity clause exists; any fundamental-law provision can be changed via the two-identical-decisions-with-an-intervening-election procedure.

Art. 8(1) states 'All human beings are equal before the law,' with Art. 8(2) barring discrimination on grounds including origin, race, religion — about as clean a universal-personhood formulation as exists in this survey. Still UNKNOWN: Arts. 192-194 explicitly permit total revision of the entire Constitution (including Art. 8) via popular initiative and double-majority referendum, with only external jus cogens as a hard limit, not any domestic eternity clause. Flagged only because its wording is unusually strong even though it fails prong (b) cleanly.

Art. 157 bars amendments that "abolish or restrict" human and citizens' rights (broader than most — covers both categories) and bars amendment during martial law — but this is a non-narrowing ratchet under an ordinary, existing amendment procedure (Arts. 155–156), not an absolute bar on touching the clause; a domestic path exists, just constrained in direction.

The UK has no single codified constitution; under parliamentary sovereignty, no statute (Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010, or otherwise) is legally entrenched, and any Act of Parliament can be amended or repealed by a simple majority, with no Parliament able to bind its successors — a clean, easy UNKNOWN since no entrenched provisions of any kind exist.

Charter s.15(1) uses universal 'every individual' language, but it carries no special entrenchment: it amends under the general 7/50 procedure (Part V, s.38) of the Constitution Act 1982, not the narrow unanimity list in s.41 (monarchy, SCC, amending formula itself). A clear, easy domestic amendment path exists.

14th Amendment Equal Protection Clause uses universal 'any person' wording, but Article V's entrenchment covers only the narrow equal-state-suffrage-in-the-Senate clause, not equal protection. Equal protection is fully amendable via ordinary Article V (2/3 Congress + 3/4 states, or convention).

Article 1 guarantees human rights to 'todas las personas' and bars discrimination based on ethnic/national origin, among other grounds — universal wording. Amendment under Article 135 (2/3 of Congress plus a majority of state legislatures) has no exempted/unamendable articles, so Article 1 is fully reformable.

Chapter II protects 'the individual' against discrimination by race, place of origin, political opinion, colour, creed or sex (s.16). Belize's fundamental-rights chapter is 'specially entrenched' under s.69, requiring a 3/4 National Assembly vote plus a national referendum — a demanding but real domestic path.

Article 33 states 'toda persona es igual ante la ley' and bars discrimination contrary to human dignity — universal wording. Amendment proceeds either as a full revision via Constituent Assembly or a partial reform by the Legislative Assembly over two sessions; no clause is permanently shielded.

Article 3 declares all persons equal before the law without distinction by nationality, race, sex or religion — universal wording. Article 248 entrenches only the principle of non-reelection/alternability of the presidency; the equality clause is not on that list and reforms through the ordinary two-legislature process.

Article 4 states 'todos los seres humanos son libres e iguales en dignidad y derechos' — strongly universal wording. Reform via a Constituent Assembly remains a domestic path even for Title I/II provisions; Article 281's absolute bar covers only a narrow list (republican form, presidential non-reelection) that does not include Art. 4.
Art. 374 entrenches only the form of government, territory, and presidential term/no-reelection provisions — no equality or rights content of any kind is entrenched.

Article 27 guarantees equality before the law to 'todas las personas' without distinction by birth, nationality, creed, race, sex, language, religion, opinion, origin, or condition — universal wording. Total reform requires a Constituent Assembly and partial reform a supermajority across two legislatures; nothing is permanently unamendable.

Article 19 bars privileges or discrimination based on race, birth, disability, social class, sex, religion or political ideas — phrased universally. Title XIII reform (two consecutive legislatures, or a constituent assembly via referendum) contains no permanently unamendable provisions.

Chapter II's non-discrimination clause (s.14) is part of the 'specially entrenched' fundamental-rights chapter: amendment requires a 2/3 vote of both Houses plus a national referendum. A referendum path, however demanding, still exists domestically.

Chapter III protects persons 'whatever his race, place of origin, political opinions, colour, creed or sex' (Art. 15 preamble; Art. 26), though with notable historical gaps (e.g. a failed 2016 gender-equality referendum). Entrenched/specially entrenched provisions require a referendum to alter (Art. 54), so a domestic path exists.

Chapter III non-discrimination clause (s.23) sits among the Constitution's entrenched provisions, alterable by a 2/3 majority of both Houses of Parliament (s.49) — a parliamentary supermajority path exists with no absolute bar.

The 2019 Constitution's Article 41 is unusually broad and universal: 'todas las personas son iguales ante la ley,' barring discrimination on an extensive list of grounds. Reform (Title XIII) requires National Assembly approval and, for core chapters, a mandatory referendum — a demanding but existing domestic path, with no article rendered absolutely unamendable.

Chapter I's non-discrimination clause (s.13) falls within the 'specially entrenched' category, alterable only by a 3/4 House of Assembly vote plus a mandatory national referendum. A domestic (if onerous) amendment path exists.

Article 39 states all persons are 'born free and equal before the law' and bars discrimination on an extensive list of grounds — strongly universal. Reform proceeds via a Revisory National Assembly with no permanently unamendable clauses.

Chapter I's non-discrimination clause (s.13) is among the 'deeply entrenched' provisions requiring special parliamentary majorities plus a national referendum to amend. A domestic path exists despite the high bar.

Article 18 states 'Tous les Haïtiens sont égaux devant la loi' — limited to Haitian citizens, failing universality regardless of entrenchment. Article 284's unamendability protections cover the republican/democratic form of government, not the citizen-limited equality clause.

The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (2011) secures rights to 'every person' and bars discrimination on broad grounds (s.13) — universal wording. 'Deeply entrenched' provisions, which include the Charter, require special parliamentary majorities and a referendum to amend, so a domestic path still exists.
Chapter II's non-discrimination clause (s.15) is an entrenched provision requiring a 2/3 National Assembly vote plus a national referendum to amend — a demanding but real domestic path.
Chapter I's non-discrimination clause (s.13) sits among the Constitution's specially entrenched provisions, amendable via special parliamentary majority plus referendum — a domestic path exists.

Chapter I's non-discrimination clause (s.13) is an entrenched provision requiring a 2/3 House of Assembly vote plus a national referendum for the specially entrenched category — a domestic path exists.

Section 4(b) recognizes 'the right of the individual to equality before the law,' with s.4(d) barring discrimination by race, origin, colour, religion or sex — broadly universal. Unusually, Trinidad and Tobago requires no referendum: most of Chapter 1 (including s.4) amends via a 3/5 parliamentary supermajority — a clear existing domestic path.

Article 16 declares 'todos sus habitantes son iguales ante la ley' — applying to all inhabitants, not just citizens, so universal. Amendment under Article 30 proceeds via a Convención Constituyente called by 2/3 of Congress; no article is textually unamendable, though some scholars argue an implicit 'clausula petrea' protects the republican form (not equality specifically).

Article 14.II broadly bars discrimination against 'toda persona' on an extensive list of grounds. Total reform requires an originating Constituent Assembly activated by referendum, and partial reform proceeds via Congress and/or referendum — demanding but existing domestic paths, with no eternity clause.

Art. 60 §4 entrenches "individual rights and guarantees" generally. Art. 5's equality clause reads "all are equal before the law, without distinction of any kind, guaranteeing to Brazilians and foreigners residing in the country..." — broader than citizens-only (covers resident foreigners) but not phrased as unconditionally universal. A genuine middle case; not confirmed to satisfy §6.9.2(b) as written.

Article 1 states 'las personas nacen libres e iguales en dignidad y derechos' — universal wording. The amendment chapter requires 3/5 or 2/3 congressional supermajorities depending on the chapter but contains no entrenched/unamendable core, unlike Germany's Art. 79(3) model.

Article 13 guarantees that 'todas las personas nacen libres e iguales ante la ley' with an extensive non-discrimination list — universal. Reform proceeds via Congress, popular referendum, or a Constituent Assembly; the Constitutional Court's judicially-created 'sustitución de constitución' doctrine limits reforms that replace the Constitution's core but is not a textual absolute bar.

Article 11(2) broadly guarantees equality for 'todas las personas' on an extensive list of grounds — universal and expansive. The three-tier amendment system requires the more demanding reforma parcial or full Constituent Assembly route for provisions affecting rights and guarantees, but a domestic path still exists at that higher tier; no article is absolutely unamendable.

Article 149 prohibits discriminatory laws on grounds including race, place of origin, political opinion, colour, creed and sex, in the standard Commonwealth Caribbean 'no person' universal style. Altering entrenched provisions requires a 2/3 National Assembly vote, and for the most entrenched matters also a national referendum — a domestic path exists.

Article 46 states 'todos los habitantes de la República son iguales en dignidad y derechos' — universal wording covering inhabitants generally. Article 290 lists a narrow set of matters excluded from the simplified amendment procedure, but Article 46 is not among those exceptions and nothing is permanently unamendable.

Article 2(2) guarantees 'toda persona' equality before the law with an extensive grounds list — universal. Amendment under Article 206 proceeds via either two successive ordinary legislatures' approval or a 2/3 congressional vote plus referendum; no eternity clause exists.

Article 8(2) bars discrimination against anyone on grounds of birth, sex, race, language, religious origin, education, political conviction, economic position or other status — universal. Amendment requires only a 2/3 National Assembly supermajority, with no referendum requirement or unamendable core — a comparatively easy domestic path exists.

Article 8 declares 'todas las personas son iguales ante la ley' — universal, with no distinctions recognized other than talents or virtues. Article 331 offers multiple amendment routes; none of them is barred from reaching the equality clause.

Article 21 guarantees 'todas las personas' equality before the law and bars discrimination by race, sex, creed or social condition — universal. Title IX provides three escalating reform routes, including a plenary-powers Constituent Assembly treated in Venezuelan doctrine as holding unlimited 'originario' constituent power, meaning no article, including Art. 21, is shielded from eventual domestic revision.

The Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 contains no general bill of rights and no equality-before-the-law clause at all. The only amendment mechanism is s.128 (Parliament + national referendum) and it applies to every part of the document — there is no unamendable/eternity provision. Since there is no qualifying clause to test, this is a clean, fast UNKNOWN.

Article 26 of the 2013 Constitution states 'Every person is equal before the law' — clearly universal wording. The Fiji Supreme Court's August 2025 advisory opinion read the amendment threshold down to two-thirds of Parliament plus a simple-majority referendum, and confirmed Article 26 is not among the handful of provisions held genuinely unamendable — historically the most rigid case in the set, but still disqualifying.

Article 15 bars discriminatory laws applying to 'no person' — universal wording. Article 69 allows alteration of the entire Constitution, including Chapter II, via a two-thirds vote of Parliament plus, for Chapter II specifically, a nationwide referendum — a heightened procedural bar, not an absolute prohibition.

Article II, §12(1) states 'All persons are equal under the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the laws' — squarely universal wording. Article XII provides two amendment routes (Nitijela resolution + referendum, or constitutional convention + referendum); no provision designates any article as absolutely unamendable.

Article IV, §4 provides equal protection 'without denial or impairment on account of sex, race, ancestry, national origin, language, or social status,' applying to persons generally. Article XIV sets amendment at three-fourths of votes cast in three-fourths of the states; no eternity clause was found, and §4 is not singled out for special protection.

Article 3 guarantees fundamental rights to 'every person in Nauru... whatever his race, place of origin, political opinions, colour, creed or sex' — universal wording. Article 84's enhanced entrenchment (Fifth Schedule) does not include Article 3, so the core equality clause is amendable by ordinary two-thirds vote alone.

New Zealand has no single codified or entrenched constitution; its order is an uncodified mix of statutes, the Treaty of Waitangi, and convention, all under parliamentary sovereignty. Equality provisions in the Bill of Rights Act and Human Rights Act are ordinary statutes repealable by simple majority — no entrenchment mechanism exists, a straightforward UNKNOWN by the system's structure.

Article IV, §5 states 'Every person shall be equal under the law and shall be entitled to equal protection' — universal wording. Article XIV offers three amendment routes, each followed by referendum ratification; no eternity clause was found, so §5 is amendable through any of these ordinary paths.

Section 55, the specific equality clause, is limited to 'all citizens' — narrower than universal-persons wording, though the broader Basic Rights division generally speaks of 'every person.' Basic Rights receive heightened but not absolute protection — no provision makes s.55 completely unamendable.

Article 15 states 'All persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection under the law' — universal wording, confirmed against the official text. Amendment is via a two-thirds majority of the Legislative Assembly with no heightened threshold specific to fundamental rights or any eternity clause; amendments have reportedly been passed frequently.

Section 15 (Chapter II) protects against discriminatory treatment on grounds including race, place of origin, political opinion, colour, creed and sex. Section 61 entrenches Chapter II behind a three-quarters-of-all-members threshold on two readings — one of the more rigid entrenchment schemes in the set, but a domestic path (the 3/4 vote) plainly still exists.

Clause 4 ('Same Law for All Classes') declares one law for chiefs, commoners, non-Tongans and Tongans alike — an old but broadly universal equality formula, though it predates modern categories like religion or ethnicity. Clause 79 shields only royal succession and noble titles/estates from amendment — Clause 4 is not on that protected list.

Section 27 protects 'no-one' from discriminatory treatment on race, place of origin, political opinion, colour or religious belief — universal wording. Amendment requires only a two-thirds majority of Parliament with no referendum requirement or eternity clause found; a 2023 amendment entrenched statehood/maritime boundaries but this is unrelated to the equality clause.

Article 5(1) grants fundamental rights and freedoms 'without discrimination on the grounds of race, place of origin, religious or traditional beliefs, political opinions, language or sex' to 'all persons,' expressly including non-citizens — universal wording. No eternity clause was found; Article 5(1) is amendable via the ordinary two-thirds parliamentary route.
